Comparing the impact of thermal stresses and bubble pressure on intergranular fracture in UO2 using 2D phase field fracture simulations

Abstract

UO2 fuel fragmentation and pulverization during loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCAs) is an ongoing safety concern that has gained importance due to recent interest in increasing burnup limits for light water reactor fuel. In this work, we investigate the importance of bubble pressure on fragmentation using 2D phase field fracture simulations of UO2 polycrystals. The model includes anisotropic single crystal elastic constants, encourages intergranular fracture, and includes bubble pressure and its impact on crack opening. An external stress is applied that is representative of the internal stresses observed in macroscale BISON simulations of LOCA tests. Cracks do not form under the external applied stress in UO2 polycrystals without porosity. Crack nucleation and propagation do occur under the external applied stress in polycrystals with unpressurized 1 μm radius intergranular voids, and crack propagation accelerates with increasing number of voids. Crack nucleation and propagation also occur in polycrystals without the external applied stress if the intergranular pores are pressurized, and crack propagation is faster with both pressurized pores and the external applied stress. Our 2D results indicate that bubble pressure may not be necessary to initiate fragmentation in polycrystals with intergranular porosity under LOCA conditions, though this should be verified using 3D simulations with fewer assumptions.

1. Introduction

Uranium dioxide (UO2) is a brittle ceramic that tends to fracture during normal operation and transients [1], [2], [3], [4]. Thus, light water reactor (LWR) fuel pellets always contain cracks during reactor operation. They fracture during standard operational increases in power, such as reactor startup (primarily radial cracks), and decreases in power (primarily circumferential cracks) [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10]. These macroscale cracks impact fuel performance by reducing the internal stress state of the fuel and resulting in some relocation that decreases the gap width [11]. During accident conditions, additional fracture mechanisms have been observed in UO2: fuel fragmentation and pulverization [11]. Rapid temperature changes, such as rapid heating during a reactivity-insertion accident (RIA) [12] or loss-of-coolant accident (LOCA) [13] or rapid cooling due to fuel quenching during a LOCA [14], cause fine cracks to form near the outer radius of the pellet in a behavior typically called fragmentation. In addition, once fission gas bubbles form within the fuel, rapid temperature changes can result in extensive cracking at grain boundaries, forming very small fuel particles (on the order of the grain size) [15], [16], [17]. This process is typically called pulverization (or fine fragmentation) and is generally accompanied by significant fission gas release. It is hypothesized that the stresses that develop in the pellet due to thermal expansion and contraction cause fragmentation [18] and that rapid pressure changes in the bubbles cause pulverization [16], [17], [18]. Fragmentation and especially pulverization result in very small fuel fragments that can escape through cladding ruptures, entering the coolant and significantly increasing the negative consequences of an accident.
With industry’s desire to raise the burnup limit of LWR fuel, there has been a renewed interest in understanding fuel fragmentation and pulverization due to its potential impact on fuel safety as fuel burnup increases. Two recent scoping studies were carried out using fuel samples irradiated to a local burnup of 71 MWd/kgU, one investigating the impact of hydrostatic pressure using rapid annealing tests, and one in which laser heating was carried out on small samples [19]. The results of these studies were used to develop a temperature and burnup threshold for fuel pulverization. More recently, new tests were carried out at Oak Ridge National Laboratory [20] and their results were compared with this threshold. The threshold was conservative for all but two of their experiments and was later used in the BISON fuel performance code to develop a methodology to evaluate high-burnup fuel susceptibility to pulverization during a LOCA [21].
The pulverization threshold [19] provides an approach to evaluate the susceptibility of fuel pellets to pulverization under various conditions, as illustrated by Capps et al. [21]. However, this threshold is a simplification of the phenomenon, as noted in the original work [19]. The authors demonstrated an influence of temperature ramp rate, hydrostatic pressure, and the formation of high-burnup structure that are not included in the pulverization threshold. Note that high-burnup structure is a fuel reconstructing phenomenon resulting in nanocrystalline grains surrounding larger than 1 μm radius fission gas bubbles [22] Thus, an additional investigation of pulverization and its causes is warranted.
The phase field fracture model is a simulation approach in which a continuous damage field is used to represent the nucleation and propagation of discrete cracks in brittle materials. It has has been demonstrated to be a useful tool for investigating the impact of fuel microstructure on its fracture behavior. This approach was first applied to UO2 by Chakraborty et al. [23] to investigate the impact of fission gas bubbles on intergranular fracture of UO2 using 2D simulations. This approach was later used to investigate the same behavior using 3D simulations [24]. Recently, a quasi-brittle phase field fracture model for pressurized cracks was used to simulate fission-gas-induced fragmentation of the UO2 high-burnup structure [25].
In this work, we have applied the phase field fracture method to compare the impact of thermal stresses and bubble pressure on the fracture of UO2 microstructures under LOCA conditions, in an effort to better understand the causes of fragmentation and pulverization. We only considered fuel that has not undergone grain subdivision to form the high-burnup structure (HBS), such that we used average grain sizes on the order of 10 μm. We first summarize the phase field fracture model used in this work and discuss how it was calibrated to model UO2. We then apply the model to investigate the microcracking of UO2 under LOCA conditions.

2. Phase field fracture model

We simulate the fracture of UO2 following the model from Zhang et. al [26]. In the phase field fracture model, the crack is represented by a continuous variable field 𝑑, where 𝑑=1 in a crack, 𝑑=0 in intact material, and 𝑑 smoothly transitions from 0 to 1 on either side of the crack. 𝑑 evolves to minimize the total free energy of the system. Here, we summarize the equation that defines the evolution of 𝑑, the mechanics model, and how fission gas bubbles are included in the model.

2.1. Phase field evolution equation

The total free energy in the phase field fracture model is a sum of fracture and strain energy. The fracture energy is smeared across the crack according to(1)𝐹𝑓⁡𝑟⁢𝑎⁢𝑐=∫Ω𝐺𝑐⁡(𝑑22⁢𝑙+𝑙2⁢|𝛻𝑑|2)𝑑Ω,where 𝐺𝑐 is the critical energy release rate and 𝑙 represents the crack thickness [27]. The strain energy density is decomposed into the portion that contributes to crack propagation,𝜓+ and the portion that does not, 𝜓−; thus,(2)𝐹𝑠⁢𝑡⁢𝑟⁢𝑎⁢𝑖⁢𝑛=∫Ωℎ⁡(𝑑)⁢𝜓++𝜓−𝑑Ω,where ℎ⁡(𝑑)=(1−𝑑)2⁢(1−𝑘)+𝑘 with 𝑘≪1 to improve convergence. The total free energy in damaged material is(3)𝐹=∫Ωℎ⁡(𝑑)⁢𝜓++𝜓−+𝐺𝑐⁡(𝑑22⁢𝑙+𝑙2⁢|𝛻𝑑|2)𝑑Ω.
The crack variable 𝑑 evolves to decrease the total free energy in the system. Its evolution is defined using a modified Allen-Cahn equation(4)𝜕𝑑𝜕𝑡=−𝐿⁢𝛿⁢𝐹𝛿⁢𝑑=−𝐿⁢(𝜕ℎ𝜕𝑑⁢𝜓++𝐺𝑐⁡(𝑑𝑙−𝑙⁢Δ⁢𝑑)),where L is the Allen-Cahn mobility parameter.

2.2. Mechanics model

Due to the brittle behavior of UO2, small deformation is assumed, so the strain tensor ɛ is a linear function of displacement 𝒖:(5)ɛ=12⁢(𝛻𝒖+𝛻𝒖𝑇).We assume linear elasticity, such that the intact stress tensor 𝛔0 is a linear function of the elasticity tensor 𝑪,(6)𝛔0=𝑪⁢ɛ.Elasticity tensors with any symmetry can be used.
There are various methods to decompose the deformation energy to determine 𝜓+ and 𝜓−; these methods were reviewed and compared in previous work of the authors [28]. In this work, we use the spectral stress decomposition approach from Zhang et al. [26] in which the stress is decomposed into positive and negative parts based on the eigen-decomposition of the stress tensor:(7)𝛔±=𝑸⁢𝚲±⁢𝑸𝑇,where 𝑸 is a matrix containing the eigenvectors of the intact stress tensor 𝛔0. 𝚲 is a diagonal matrix containing the eigenvalues, and 𝚲± are matrices where only the positive/negative eigenvalues are nonzero. The strain energy density is decomposed according to(8)𝜓±=12⁢𝛔±:𝛜.The total stress in damaged material is(9)𝛔=ℎ⁡(𝑑)⁢𝛔++𝛔−,and the equilibrium equation assuming quasi-static conditions in the system is(10)𝛻·𝛔=0.

2.3. Mechanical behavior of fission gas bubbles

Fission gas bubbles are represented by the static variable field 𝜂, where 𝜂=1 in a bubble, 𝜂=0 within the UO2, and 0<𝜂<1 across the bubble surface that is represented with a finite width. We assume stress is zero inside of a bubble, such that the elasticity tensor(11)𝓒=𝓒0⁢𝑔⁡(𝜂),where 𝓒0 is the elasticity tensor of UO2 and the switching function(12)𝑔⁡(𝜂)=3⁢𝜂2−2⁢𝜂3.
Fission gas bubbles are also under pressure due to the gas atoms within the pore, and this pressure can contribute to fracture. We represent the pressure in the phase field fracture model by adding a regularized external work to the total free energy:(13)𝐹=∫Ωℎ⁡(𝑑)⁢𝜓++𝜓−+𝐺𝑐⁡(𝑑22⁢𝑙+𝑙2⁢|𝛻𝑑|2)−𝑝⁢2⁢𝑑⁢(𝛻𝑑·𝒖)⁢𝑑⁢Ω,where 𝑝 is the pressure applied on the crack surfaces. The detailed derivation of the pressure term can be found in [25]. The stress equilibrium equation, Eq.  (10), is modified as:(14)𝛻·𝛔−𝑝⁢2⁢𝑑𝛻𝑑=0.

3. Model implementation and simulation methodology

In order to compare the impact of fuel stresses and bubble pressure on fracture in UO2 during LOCA conditions, we implement the phase field fracture model summarized in the previous section. Eqs.  (4) and (14) are solved using the finite element method with the Multiphysics Object-Oriented Simulation Environment(MOOSE) [23], [24], [29], [30], [31], which is an open-source software to solve multi-physics coupled problems. MOOSE has been successfully used to implement phase field fracture models [23], [24], [26], [28], [32], and we build on that work. Here, we summarize the model parameters, demonstrate the impact of bubble pressure on fracture, and determine a stress state and bubble pressures representative of LOCA conditions to apply to the UO2 polycrystals.

3.1. Model parameter selection for UO2

In this work, we apply the phase field fracture model to simulate cracking in UO2 polycrystals under LOCA conditions. The past application of the phase field fracture model for UO2 in 2D [23] and 3D [24] investigated the impact of fission gas bubbles on the fracture strength of UO2. They assumed quasi-static mechanical behavior, intergranular fracture, and isotropic elastic response of the UO2 grains. They defined the critical energy release rate 𝐺𝑐 for UO2 by comparing to atomic-scale simulations carried out using molecular dynamics (MD). This resulted in a larger fracture strength for UO2 than has been seen in previous experiments, since the MD simulations assume a perfect material without defects or impurities.
The fluorite crystal structure of UO2 has cubic symmetry, and therefore, the single crystal elastic response must be represented by three unique elastic constants, rather than the two isotropic elastic constants assumed in past work [23], [24]. We use single crystal elastic constants measured at room temperature [33], since high temperature single crystal elastic constants are not available. The three elastic constants used in this work are 𝒞11=395 GPa, 𝒞12=121 GPa, and 𝒞44=64.1 GPa.
We determined the 𝐺𝑐 value for UO2 by comparing it to experimental data, rather than MD simulation results. Oguma [2] carried out biaxial flexure experiments on UO2 at room temperature and determined how the fracture stress changed as a function of grain size, porosity, and pore size. Oguma found that the UO2 fracture strength, taken as the maximum tensile stress without pores and with an average grain size ranging from 8 to 16 μm, was 133 MPa. Recent experimental work by Doitrand et al. [34] used single crystal micro-cantilever experiments and finite element fracture mechanics simulations to determine the energy release rate and fracture stress of single crystal UO2. They obtained fracture stresses around 2 GPa and 𝐺𝑐 values from 8 to 10 J/m2 for fresh UO2 and 5 J/m2 for irradiated UO2. The fracture stress from the micro-cantilever samples from Doitrand et al. was much higher than from the bulk polycrystal samples from Oguma likely due to grain boundaries and other defects that weaken the material. We fitted the grain boundary 𝐺𝑐 value for the phase field fracture simulations by comparing it to bulk polycrystal experimental value from Oguma, since we are investigating fracture of polycrystalline samples.
The value for 𝐺𝑐 cannot be directly obtained from the experimental fracture stress, since 𝐺𝑐 is independent of the defect structures while the fracture stress is highly sensitive to them. Therefore, we carried out a calibration process in which we ran various simulations with different values of 𝐺𝑐 along the grain boundaries until we found a value that resulted in a fracture strength similar to the 133 MPa from the experiments. We used a 50 μm by 50 μm 2D polycrystal with 25 grains generated using a Voronoi tessellation, such that the average grain size was 11.3 μm, where the average grain size is the diameter of an equivalent circle with the average grain area. The grains had randomly distributed planar crystal orientations ranging from 0∘ to 90∘. We assumed that the fracture would be primarily intergranular, so we used a 𝐺𝑐 ten times larger within the grains than on the grain boundaries as was done in the past mesoscale phase field fracture simulations of UO2 [23], [24]. The polycrystal was loaded in uniaxial tension to best reproduce the maximum tensile stress reported by Oguma. This was achieved with an applied 𝑦-displacement on the top boundary and symmetry boundary conditions on the left and bottom boundaries. An example of the final cracked polycrystal is shown in Fig. 1a. The length parameter is set as 𝑙=0.2μm, and the element mesh size is 0.1μm. We obtained a reasonable fracture stress with a grain boundary energy release rate of 𝐺𝑐=0.1 J/m2, as demonstrated in the stress strain curve in Fig. 1b. This critical energy release rate value obtained by comparing to the experimental data is much smaller than the value of 𝐺𝑐=2.0 J/m2 obtained by comparing to the MD simulation data in the previous work [23].
The final value needed for the phase field fracture model is the Allen-Cahn mobility 𝐿. Dynamic phase field fracture methods are needed for very high strain rates, though quasi-static methods are sufficient for most cases [28]. For the strain rates used in this work, we found that a quasi-static method gave the same results as a dynamic method and for less computational cost. Thus, we use a quasi-state method that can assume that 𝜕𝑑/𝜕𝑡=0 in Eq.  (4) and solve for the steady-state condition. However, this makes the nonlinear system of equations harder to solve. Therefore, we assume 𝜕𝑑/𝜕𝑡>0 but select a value of 𝐿 that is large enough to have little impact on the problem solution. For this work, we find that 𝐿=1×106⁢𝐺⁡𝑃⁢𝑎/𝑠 is large enough to have negligible impact on the evolution of 𝑑 but also not hurt the non-linear convergence. For more details on the impact of 𝐿 on the solution, see Chakraborty et al.  [23].

3.2. Demonstration of the impact of bubble pressure

A critical part of this work is to investigate the impact of bubble pressure on fracture in UO2 during LOCA conditions, where pressure is added to the fracture model using the approach discussed in Section 2.3. Here, we demonstrate the impact of the bubble pressure using a simple 10 μm by 10 μm single crystal geometry (oriented 0∘ from the 𝑥-axis) with a single bubble located at the center of the domain. We model the crack initiation and growth with different bubble radii in which the bubble pressure linearly increases as a function of time (i.e., 𝑃=80⁢𝑡 GPa). For this demonstration, we use symmetry boundary conditions on the left and bottom boundaries. Note that the crack paths would be somewhat altered with different boundary conditions.
The cracked domain shaded by the hydrostatic pressure for bubble sizes ranging from 0.5μm to 2μm with an interval of 0.5μm are shown in Figs. 2(a) - 2(d). The crack length versus time for the various bubbles sizes is shown in Fig. 2(e). Cracks nucleate at the pore and radiate outward towards the domain boundaries. With increasing pore radius, cracks nucleate at decreasing pressures and propagate at increasing rates. These results show that the pressure induces tensile stresses around the pores that causes crack nucleation. The pressure then propagates down the cracks, continuing to force them open and accelerating their propagation, since we assume constant pressure in the cracks.

3.3. Determination of the LOCA stress state

In order to compare the impact of internal stress and bubble pressure on fracture in UO2 during a LOCA, we must know the internal stress state during a LOCA. The stress state cannot be easily obtained experimentally but can be obtained from fuel performance simulations using tools such as BISON [35], [36]. The capabilities of BISON for LOCA fuel behavior has been validated using existing data from LOCA tests carried out by Studsvik and Halden [37], [38]. It has also been used to model the fuel behaviors during an actual LOCA and evaluate the pulverization behavior [21], [39]. Therefore, in this work we use BISON results to provide guidance on the stress state we should use in our phase field fracture simulations.
To determine the stress inside a pellet during a LOCA, we are relying on the BISON results from a Studsvik LOCA test case [40], [41]. Specifically, we use the results from Rods 191 and 196. The various materials models used in the simulations are the same as used in past LOCA simulations [37], [38], including models for pellet-fragment radial relocation, isotropic softening due to cracking, and fuel creep.
The centerline temperature in the refabricated rodlets in the Studsvik LOCA test are shown in Figs. 3a and 3e. Due to the rapid temperature change just after 1000 s, there is a jump in the stress throughout the pellet. At the center of the rod, the stresses are all tensile, with the axial stress being the largest (Figs. 3b and 3f). At the mid-radius (Figs. 3c and 3g), the hoop stress is initially compressive and then jumps to be tensile after the temperature increase. The axial stress is again the largest. At the pellet periphery (Figs. 3d and 3h), the axial and hoop stresses are always compressive, though they go down after the temperature increase. The radial stress goes from compressive to tensile after the temperature jump. The largest changes in the stresses occur very quickly, within 1 ms.
Our phase field fracture simulations are 2D approximations of a small square section of material within the fuel. We apply a tensile stress 𝜎𝐴 to the square domain that is similar to the local stress states within the pellet. The maximum tensile stress experienced in the fuel during the LOCA test was 64 MPa. Therefore, 𝜎𝐴 linearly increases from 0 to 66 MPa within 1 ms and then slightly increases at 2 MPa/ms (see Fig. 4a). The small secondary slope is used because it results in better numerical convergence than holding 𝜎𝐴 constant. 𝜎𝐴 is applied on the right boundary. Symmetry boundary conditions are used on the left and bottom boundaries. The boundary conditions are shown in Fig. 4(b). Note that these boundary conditions are simple and do not represent the full stress state that may be experienced within a fuel pellet during a LOCA.

3.4. Fission gas bubble pressures during a LOCA

Fission gas bubbles are voids filled with fission gas. The large bubbles that grow and interconnect on grain boundaries are typically at equilibrium pressure during normal reactor operation, since sufficient vacancies can diffuse to the bubbles and allow them to grow to decrease the pressure [42], [43]. During a LOCA, rapid temperature changes in the fuel rapidly change the pressure in the bubble, and there is not sufficient time for additional vacancy diffusion to equilibrate the pressure. These rapid pressure changes cause an additional driving force for fracture and can result in rapid fission gas release, often called transient fission gas release or burst release [18], [42]. Previous work using the finite element method with cohesive zone elements investigated grain boundary fracture due to bubble pressure, and it found that break-away fracture can occur when the pressure enters the crack and pushes on the crack surfaces [44]. Thus, it is critical for us to investigate the fracture behavior during a LOCA with bubble pressure that can move from the bubbles into the cracks.
To determine representative pressures to apply within the bubbles, we consider the recent work by Aagesen et al. [45]. In that work, they used a phase field model of fission gas bubble growth that included the impact of bubble pressure and bubble surface tension. They found that, during LOCA conditions, the pressure in a 250 nm radius bubble could increase by as much as 200 MPa from its initial value. To investigate the impact of bubble pressure on fracture in the 2D polycrystals, we consider two maximum bubble pressures: 𝑃1=80 MPa, less than half the value from Aagesen et al., and 𝑃2=150 MPa, 75% of their value. For each, the pressure in the bubbles increases from zero to its maximum pressure in 1 ms and is then held constant, as shown in Fig. 4(a).

4. Simulations of the fracture of UO2 polycrystals in LOCA conditions

As we mentioned in the introduction, it is currently hypothesized that pulverization results from rapid changes in bubble pressure, while fragmentation is caused by thermal stresses. In order to provide more insights on pulverization, we compare the impact of the internal stress state in the fuel pellet during a LOCA, determined in Section 3.3, with the impact of bubble pressure. We simulate the fracture behavior for three cases of 2D UO2 polycrystals with an applied load: without pores or bubbles, with unpressurized intergranular pores, and with pressurized intergranular bubbles.

4.1. Behavior of UO2 without pores or bubbles

We first simulate the behavior of UO2 with no fission gas bubbles or porosity, using 60×60 μm UO2 polycrystal domains with 36 grains, giving an average grain size of 11.3 μm. Two 2D polycrystals are generated: Case I is generated using a Voronoi tessellation (Fig. 5a) and Case II has more realistic grain shapes produced by relaxing a Voronoi tessellation using a phase field grain growth simulation [46] (Fig. 5b). Random planar crystal orientations were assigned to the grains in each and were used to rotate the UO2 single crystal elasticity tensor created from the elastic constants discussed in Section 3.1.
A heterogeneous stress state forms throughout the polycrystals, as shown in Figs. 5(c) and 5(d), due to the anisotropic single crystal behavior of UO2 and the polycrystalline structure. The stresses range from 60 to 90 MPa, with the largest and smallest stresses occurring near grain boundaries. The stress distribution is similar in Cases I and II. The polycrystals never experience enough stress to nucleate a crack. This case provides an important benchmark, illustrating that some stress concentration other than grain boundaries is needed to cause large enough stresses to induce fracture under the LOCA test conditions applied here.

4.2. Behavior of UO2 with unpressurized voids

Next, we simulate the behavior of UO2 with unpressurized intergranular voids. We again model the Case I and Case 2 polycrystals, but now we randomly place 90 circular voids with a radius of 1 μm along the grain boundaries, as shown in Figs. 6(a) and 6(b). This radius is used because it is within the range of pore sizes characterized in a large set of irradited UO2 samples with intergranular fission gas bubbles [47]. Note that the characterized intergranular bubbles were lenticular, not circular, as used here. Lenticular pores would have a higher stress concentration than circular pores, and so our results somewhat underestimate fracture due to the pores. No pressure is applied inside the voids, so the only source of stress is the applied stress on the right boundary (see Fig. 4). Note that voids within the UO2 fuel are typically left over from sintering and are not arranged along grain boundaries like those used in these simulations. The purpose of this case is to separate the impact of the stress concentration around a void from the impact of pressure that forms in a fission gas bubble during a rapid temperature increase that will be investigated in the next section.
With unpressurized voids, crack nucleation and propagation does occur in the UO2 polycrystals. The final crack paths and stress distributions for Cases I and II are shown in Figs. 6(c) and 6(d), respectively. To provide a more quantitative comparison of the crack propagation in the two cases, the total crack length is plotted versus time in Fig. 6(e). Cracks nucleate first in Case I, a little before 1 ms but then propagate slowly through the material. In Case II, cracks nucleate at 1.5 ms and begin to propagate very quickly after around 2.3 ms. Cracks nucleate at voids along grain boundaries oriented more vertically (normal to the applied stress) and then propagate in a primarily vertical direction along grain boundaries between voids. A few cracks form within grains near bubbles, but they do not propagate significantly within the grains, since we set 𝐺𝑐 to be ten times higher within grains. In Case II, cracks span nearly the entire height of the domain following as vertical a path as possible along the grain boundaries.
Having established that just having intergranular voids present in the polycrystals is sufficient to induce fracture, we also investigated the impact of the number of voids on the fracture behavior. We compared the fracture in the Case I polycrystal with 90 bubbles from the previous result with the same polycrystal but with 27 voids removed to give 63 total voids. The 63 and 90 voids correspond to a fractional coverage of grain boundaries by voids of 0.24 and 0.34, respectively. These fractional coverages fall within the lower half of the range of intergranular fission gas bubble coverages characterized in irradiated UO2 samples [47]. We model the fracture behavior for 3.5 ms.
Cracks nucleate and propagate with both 63 and 90 voids. The final crack path and stress distributions are shown for 63 and 90 voids in Figs. 7(a) and Figs. 7(b), respectively. The crack length evolution is shown in Fig. 7(b). Cracks nucleate at the same time with both 63 and 90 voids, since they are nucleating at voids that the two polycrystals have in common. The crack propagation is faster with the 90 voids, and the final crack length is larger. The voids are closer with 90, so that cracks propagate between voids more quickly. Thus, the increased grain boundary fractional coverage reduces the overall strength of the material, as has been shown from previous work using both experiments [2] and modeling [23], [24].

4.3. Behavior of UO2 with pressurized bubbles

Finally, we simulate the fracture of UO2 with pressurized gas bubbles. We simulate the fracture in the Case I polycrystal with 90 bubbles, shown in Fig. 6(a). We compare the behavior with the two maximum pressures with no applied stress (𝜎𝐴=0) and with 𝜎𝐴 changing with time as shown in Fig. 4(a).
With bubble pressure but no applied stress, cracks form along grain boundaries oriented both horizontally and vertically, as shown in Figs. 8(a) and 8(b). Also, more intragranular cracks form than in the case with just an applied load (Fig. 7(b)). The crack paths are very similar with 80 and 150 MPa max bubble pressures, but with 80 MPa, the cracks propagate much slower than with 150 MPa, as shown in the plot of the crack length versus time (Fig. 8e). With a 80 MPa max pressure, the crack propagates even slower than it does with just the applied stress. The 80 MPa pressure is below the crack strength of UO2, but after the pressure reaches its maximum value at 1 ms, there is a stress concentration large enough to nucleate cracks. Once nucleation occurs, the pressure travels down the crack and causes crack tip stresses as high as 2.5 GPa. Thus, nucleated cracks propagate until they reach another bubble. With the 150 MPa maximum pressure, crack nucleation occurs before the pressure reaches its maximum value and propagation occurs very quickly.
With bubble pressure and applied stress, cracks tend to propagate in a vertical direction, as shown in Figs. 8c and 8 d, similar to what occurs with just the applied stress (Fig. 7(b)). However, the cracks propagate much faster with the bubble pressure and applied stress than with just the applied stress (see Fig. 8e). The crack propagation with applied stress and the 80 MPa max bubble pressure propagate at nearly the same rate as with the 150 MPa max bubble pressure but no applied stress. With the applied stress and 150 MPa max bubble pressure, the cracks propagate even faster. The crack paths are very similar with the 80 MPa and 150 MPa maximum pressures and the applied load; both have some intragranular fracture through a grain separating to vertical cracks.

5. Discussion

The results from our phase field fracture simulations on 2D UO2 polycrystals under LOCA conditions use various assumptions and simplifications. In spite of these simplifications, they provide insights into the causes of fragmentation and pulverization and lay the foundation for future simulations. Here, we discuss these insights and describe possible future investigations that could be carried out using phase field fracture simulations to gain additional insights.
In our simulations of polycrystals without porosity (see Fig. 7(b)), we find that no cracking occurs from an applied stress representative of the pellet stress state during a LOCA. These results are consistent with those from Capps et al. [39], in which they found that the macroscale stress state of the fuel during a LOCA was not sufficient to cause fracture. Thus, fresh and low burnup fuel is not likely to experience fragmentation or pulverization during a LOCA.
However, in our simulations of polycrystals with intergranular unpressurized voids, significant fracture does occur. In fact, by comparing Fig. with Fig. 8e, we see that longer cracks form after 3.5 seconds in both the Case I and Case II microstructures with unpressurized voids than in Case I with an 80 MPa bubble pressure with no applied stress. Although, with a 150 MPa pressure or with pressure and an applied stress of 80 or 150 MPa, the cracks propagated faster than in the unpressurized case. This finding indicates that the hypothesis that pulverization results from fission gas bubble pressure may not be complete, as just the presence of intergranular pores with an applied stress typical of LOCA conditions is enough to generate large amounts of cracking.
While the applied stress was sufficient to generate cracking even with unpressurized voids, it results from void structures fairly unique to fission gas bubbles. We randomly placed voids along grain boundaries using radius and fractional coverages typical for intergranular fission gas bubbles [47], and, as shown in Fig. 6, the cracks initiate at voids and then propagate along grain boundaries between voids. Such a structure is unique to intergranular gas bubbles that form in the hotter regions of fuel pellets and will therefore always be accompanied with gas pressure. The pore structures in fresh fuel pellets left after sintering typically have large isolated pores at triple junctions and would likely not result in the fracture behavior observed in our results. Thus, while our results indicate that intergranular porosity can result in significant cracking under LOCA conditions, such porosity will likely be pressurized, similar to results with bubble pressure and an applied stress (Fig. 8).
Our results provide preliminary insights with regards to the mechanisms driving fragmentation and pulverization in LWR fuel pellets during accident conditions. However, the additional use of phase field fracture simulations to investigate these phenomenon is warranted. First, our simulations were carried out in 2D, to reduce the computational cost, but the material behavior in 3D will most certainly be different than what we observed in 2D. Thus, 3D simulations should be carried out to identify possible 3D effects. In addition, we ran our simulations for a set amount of time and observed the cracking behavior. It may be insightful to run future simulations until crack propagation stops and compare the extent of fracture that occurs in various conditions. We used a single pore radius and circular bubbles, while true fission gas bubbles are catenoid shape and the radii will vary between bubbles and radiation conditions. Future simulations should use more realistic bubble shapes and randomly vary the radii to obtain more realistic conditions. Finally, we only considered grain structures with an average grain size of around 10 μm. However, it has been clearly established that the pulverization behavior is different in high-burnup fuel that has formed a high-burnup structure at the pellet rim [16]. Recent work applied the phase field fracture method to model crack propagation in 2D in fuel with high-burnup structure during a LOCA [25], and similar work should be carried out in 3D.

6. Conclusions

In this manuscript, we sought to gain insights into the mechanisms causing fuel fragmentation and pulverization by comparing the impact of thermal stresses representative of LOCA conditions and bubble pressure on fracture in UO2. We used a phase field fracture model in MOOSE to investigate the fracture in 2D UO2 polycrystals with an 11 μm average grain size in three specific cases: no fission gas bubbles (fresh fuel), unpressurized voids, and pressurized bubbles. The phase field fracture model accounted for the elastic anisotropy of UO2, encouraged intergranular fracture by having a smaller critical energy release rate along grain boundaries, and was calibrated by comparing to UO2 fracture data. A stress was applied to the 2D domain that was similar to the internal stresses in BISON simulations of a Studsvik LOCA test.
Fracture did not occur in fuel with no porosity, as the heterogeneous stress field that resulted from the polycrystalline texture did not increase the stress sufficiently to initiate cracks. In the simulations with unpressurized voids placed along grain boundaries, cracks nucleated at voids and propagated along grain boundaries between voids normal to the applied stress. Crack propagation was faster with larger grain boundary coverage of voids. Cracks also nucleated and propagated with pressurized bubbles and no applied stress, though they propagated in all directions and not just perpendicular to the applied stress. They propagated faster with larger bubble pressure. With bubble pressure and applied stress, the propagation was faster than either by itself and cracks again tended to propagate along grain boundaries normal to the applied stress. Thus, our results indicate that bubble pressure may not be necessary to initiate fragmentation in polycrystals with intergranular porosity under LOCA conditions.
